one_liner: Hobby register-based bytecode VM for the Type-C language; beats CPython 3.12 on three microbenchmarks, roughly matches node --jitless.
what_it_does: Type-V is the runtime for Type-C, a statically typed language whose TypeScript compiler (npm package @unlimitedsoftwareworks/type-c) emits .tcv bytecode plus a source map; the typev executable loads and runs that bytecode. It is not a drop-in for V8 or CPython: you must write Type-C, and the C API (typev_api.h, struct_api.h, array_api.h installed with the static library) is mainly for native FFI libraries loaded via dynlib, not for embedding a script engine in a host program.
how_it_is_fast: It is a register machine with typed instructions (256 registers per call frame, separate opcodes per data type and pointer-vs-value moves), so there is no dynamic type dispatch at run time and fields are reached by fixed offsets instead of property lookups. The interpreter loop uses computed-goto threaded dispatch (GCC/Clang labels-as-values table), call frames are cached in a linked list and reused instead of allocated per call, and array storage is a plain malloc'd buffer outside the GC heap. There is no JIT and, per its author, no optimization in the Type-C compiler.
when_to_use: You are already writing Type-C and need its runtime.
Studying a small C11 typed register VM with computed-goto dispatch, coroutines, closures and a generational copying GC (about 200 opcodes, handlers in one header).
Hobby or research work where beating CPython's interpreter on simple numeric loops and recursion (1.1x to 1.7x in the author's charts) is enough.
when_not_to_use: Anything production: the README states it is not production ready, not secure, not documented and not fully tested.

You need to beat V8's interpreter: in the published charts node --jitless wins fib(40) (8.32 s vs 9.91 s) and nested member access (0.494 s vs 0.689 s); Type-V leads only on the array test (0.828 s vs 0.892 s). With V8's JIT on, it is not in the same league.
Embedding a scripting language in a C/C++ host: there is no documented embedding API and the source language is a niche one with a TypeScript-hosted compiler.
Windows/MSVC targets: the dispatch loop relies on labels-as-values and the Windows CI job is commented out.
Long-running programs that allocate many short-lived arrays (see the array-buffer leak under gotchas).

integration.form: static lib (libtypev.a) plus the typev executable, built with CMake 3.25+
integration.dependencies: Vendored: libtable (MIT), yyjson, cpu_info; README also lists cwalk (MIT) and StringZilla (Apache-2.0). The Type-C compiler (TypeScript, Node.js/npm) is needed to produce bytecode.
integration.min_toolchain: C11, CMake 3.25; GCC or Clang (computed goto); CI builds Ubuntu gcc/clang and macOS clang
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (x86-64 and Apple arm64 per CI and the leak-track-mac-arm.sh script); Windows not supported in CI
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the engine round-robins multiple 'cores' (isolated processes) on one OS thread, and gc_alloc uses an unsynchronized static uid counter

gotchas: Shipped build flags work against it: CMakeLists.txt at the benchmark commit (9076ed2, 2024-11-13, whose executable name type_v matches the chart labels) and at HEAD forces -O0 -fno-inline. A default build is unoptimized; a Release build appends -O3 but keeps -fno-inline, so every opcode handler (declared static inline in instructions.h) stays an out-of-line call from the dispatch loop. Which configuration produced the charts is not stated.

Array element buffers are malloc'd outside the GC heap (core_array_alloc) and neither the minor nor the major collector frees them: only OT_USER_OBJECT gets a dealloc call when an object dies (gc.c at HEAD), so every dead array leaks its backing store.

The README's 'scavenger only, up to 1Mb' GC note is stale: HEAD has a generational copying collector that reserves two 80 MiB nursery semispaces plus an 80 MiB old region at start-up (1,310,720 cells of 64 bytes), and gc_alloc retries minor collections in a loop with no out-of-memory exit if a request cannot fit the nursery.

Benchmark plausibility cannot be checked: test.py, test.js and the Type-C sources are unpublished. The 'large array addition (100M elements), two preallocated arrays' test reports CPython at 1.307 s and node --jitless at 0.892 s on a 2 GB VM, which is fast for 100M-iteration interpreter loops and tight on memory for two 100M-element Python lists or JS arrays (my inference, not measured), so the scripts may lean on builtins or smaller sizes; the cross-language comparison is not demonstrably like-for-like.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when you are using Type-C. For a general embeddable bytecode VM, wasm3 or WAMR's fast interpreter are far more mature and benchmarked independently, and RISVM is a comparably small C/C++ register VM with a larger published lead over CPython (about 7.2x) and over Lua 5.3.
verified_claims_summary: First-party bar charts (mean execution time, added in commit 9076ed2 on 2024-11-13) on a 2-vCPU AMD EPYC (Family 25, Model 1) VM with 2 GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.1, Python 3.12.3 and Node.js 18.19.1 with --jitless: array allocation + sum 0.828 s vs node 0.892 s vs Python 1.307 s; fib(40) 9.91 s vs 8.32 s vs 11.07 s; nested member access 0.689 s vs 0.494 s vs 1.164 s. Type-V beats CPython on all three (1.12x to 1.69x, derived from page data) but beats node --jitless only on the array test (about 1.08x).
status_note: Stale since January 2025 (162 commits, 5 stars, no releases); Apache-2.0 and small enough to read, but self-described as unoptimized, insecure and untested, with build flags in its CMakeLists that disable optimization and inlining, so treat it as a study VM rather than a dependency.
